title: Computer & Internet Basics
description: Everyday digital skills: knowing your hardware, keeping files tidy, understanding the internet, and using AI safely.

stations.title: Hardware & Software
stations.summary: Hardware is what you can touch. Software you cannot touch — but it controls everything.
points: Hardware: processor (the brain), RAM (temporary desk), storage (the archive), screen and keyboard.
Software: the operating system (Windows/macOS/Linux/Android) plus the apps on top of it.
RAM is cleared when the computer is switched off; storage (SSD/HDD) keeps your data.
Restarting fixes many problems because it clears RAM and starts processes fresh.

questions.explain: An operating system is a program. Keyboards, processors, and cables are hardware.

options: Disappear when the computer is switched off
questions.explain: RAM is volatile. To keep data, write it to an SSD/HDD or save it in the cloud.

questions.prompt: From fastest to longest-term storage, the correct order is...
questions.explain: The processor is fastest, RAM sits below it, and SSD/HDD is much slower but keeps data.

cards.back: RAM is temporary (cleared on shutdown) · SSD is permanent

stations.title: Files & Backups
stations.summary: If it has no backup, it is only a matter of time before it is lost.
points: Folders are structure: Home → Documents → 2026 → Reports. Tidy from the start is easier.
The 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 copy off-site (such as the cloud).
A good file name leads with the date: 2026-03-14-sales-report.xlsx.

options: 3 hours of backup, twice a day, once a week
questions.explain: So that if one medium fails or one place is hit by disaster, the data survives.

questions.prompt: A file named 'report.pdf' most likely contains...
questions.explain: .pdf is the Portable Document Format, used so documents look the same on any device.

questions.prompt: Which file name is easiest to find again later?
questions.explain: A leading date sorts files automatically; keywords explain the contents.

stations.title: How the Internet Works
stations.summary: At heart the internet is three things: addresses, routes, and rules for moving data.
points: An IP address is a device's address on the network; DNS is the phonebook that turns a site name into an IP.
Bandwidth is the width of the road (how much data at once); latency is the travel time (how fast it responds).
Wi-Fi is only the way you join the local network; 'no internet' is different from 'weak Wi-Fi'.
HTTPS (the padlock) encrypts the route — it does not prove the site is honest.

questions.prompt: The job of DNS is to...
options: Translate a site name into an IP address
questions.explain: DNS is the internet's phonebook: you type 'example.com' and DNS finds its IP address.

questions.prompt: A video call keeps stuttering even though download speed is high. The likely problem is...
questions.explain: Live calls are far more sensitive to latency and jitter than to raw bandwidth.

questions.prompt: The padlock icon (HTTPS) in your browser means...
options: The route between browser and site is encrypted
The site belongs to a government
questions.explain: HTTPS only secures the path. Fraudulent sites can and do use HTTPS too.

cards.back: The internet's phonebook: name → IP address
An encrypted route, not a promise of honesty

stations.title: AI Basics
stations.summary: AI is a great helper, but it does not know things — it predicts patterns. Treat it like an assistant you must check.
points: A language model (LLM) works by predicting the next word from patterns in its training data.
Hallucination: an answer that sounds confident but is wrong. Always check important facts.
Never paste secrets: passwords, sensitive personal data, confidential work documents.
Use AI for drafts, explanations, and practice — the final decision stays with you.

questions.prompt: The right way to treat an AI answer on something important (medicine, law, money) is...
options: Treat it as a draft, then verify against trusted sources
Forward it to a group chat
questions.explain: AI can be confidently wrong. Verify with official sources before deciding.

questions.prompt: Which should you never paste into a public AI tool?
questions.explain: What you send to a public service may be stored on their systems. Keep secrets secret.

questions.prompt: In simple terms, a large language model works by...
options: Searching the internet every time you ask
Predicting the next words from patterns in its training data
Copying an answer out of one book
Contacting a human behind the scenes
questions.explain: An LLM does not look up facts by default — it produces the most likely text given its patterns.
